Place & Local Memory · First Cycle 2026

The Neighbourhood That Didn’t Forget

The Kokkinia Blockade, 1944

This project examines the 1944 Kokkinia Blockade and traces how the local community preserved and contested its memory through monuments, film, plaques, and commemorative practices from 1956 to the present

Nefeli AloniatiDigital exhibition / web story
Read the story ↓
The questionChaptersΕλληνικά / EnglishSources & credits
The public-history question
Who owns the memory of the Kokkinia Blockade, and how has a local community sustained that memory in public space?
Why this story matters

This story matters because the public needs to know its own history, particularly traumatic episodes such as Nazi war crimes and collective punishments like the Kokkinia Blockade. Remembering these events raises awareness about the mechanisms of fascism and occupation violence and, above all, helps ensure that societies recognize and resist the revival of such ideologies

Ελληνικά / English

Η μνήμη της Κοκκινιάς / Remembering Kokkinia

On 17 August 1944, German occupation forces and Greek collaborators surrounded Kokkinia, a working-class refugee neighbourhood whose residents had been active in the Resistance. Men were ordered to gather in Osia Xeni Square. Identified prisoners were taken to the former carpet factory’s walled grounds and executed. This place became known as the Blockade Wall.

The project follows how commemorations and monuments preserved the memory of the blockade through the Civil War, postwar anti-communism, the dictatorship and the return of democracy. It compares photographs, commemorative inscriptions and changes in local memorial practice.

Στις 17 Αυγούστου 1944, οι γερμανικές δυνάμεις Κατοχής και οι Έλληνες συνεργάτες τους περικύκλωσαν την Κοκκινιά, μια εργατική προσφυγική συνοικία με έντονη αντιστασιακή δράση. Οι άνδρες διατάχθηκαν να συγκεντρωθούν στην πλατεία της Οσίας Ξένης. Όσοι υποδείχθηκαν ως μέλη της Αντίστασης οδηγήθηκαν στον χώρο ενός πρώην ταπητουργείου και εκτελέστηκαν. Ο τόπος έγινε γνωστός ως Μάντρα του Μπλόκου.

Η εργασία παρακολουθεί τον τρόπο με τον οποίο οι εκδηλώσεις μνήμης και τα μνημεία διατήρησαν την ιστορία του Μπλόκου από τα μεταπολεμικά χρόνια έως τη Μεταπολίτευση. Εξετάζει φωτογραφίες, επιγραφές και αλλαγές στη δημόσια μνήμη της συνοικίας.

CHAPTER 01

17 August 1944: A neighbourhood surrounded

On the morning of 17 August 1944, German occupation forces and Greek collaborators sealed off Kokkinia, a working-class refugee neighbourhood with a strong Resistance presence. Men were ordered to assemble in Osia Xeni Square. Local collaborators identified people accused of resistance activity, some of whom were taken to the former carpet factory courtyard and executed. The place became known as the Blockade Wall of Kokkinia.

CHAPTER 02

Execution, detention and forced labour

The blockade brought mass executions and arrests. Prisoners were marched towards Haidari, and some were subsequently sent to Nazi Germany for forced labour. The project places these events within the occupation of Greece and the systematic persecution of communities associated with resistance. The exact number of those killed is a matter for careful source comparison.

CHAPTER 03

How the community began to commemorate

Commemoration began before the event could be fully acknowledged by state institutions. In 1956, a monument to those killed was erected in Osia Xeni Square, attributed in the submitted research to sculptor Georgios Zongolopoulos. The monument shows how local memory found public expression in a politically divided postwar Greece.

CHAPTER 04

Film, politics and the struggle over memory

The 1965 film To Bloko, directed by Adonis Kyrou, brought the events of August 1944 to a wider audience. Filmed in the area with the participation of local residents, it became another medium through which the community could preserve and communicate an account of the blockade.

CHAPTER 05

A contested inscription under the dictatorship

During the military dictatorship of 1967–1974, a commemorative inscription attributed responsibility for the killings in ways that distorted the involvement of the occupation forces and their collaborators. The author reads this intervention as evidence that memorial sites can become arenas of political struggle over historical interpretation.

CHAPTER 06

After 1974: Recognition and reinterpretation

With the restoration of democracy in 1974, the place of the Resistance in Greek public life became a subject of renewed discussion. The memory of the blockade gained increased institutional recognition during the 1980s, alongside wider debates about occupation, collaboration and civil conflict.

CHAPTER 07

A network of places, plaques and testimonies

Municipal plaques and commemorative practices marked streets and sites connected with the blockade. Together they make an unofficial geography of resistance visible, allowing residents and visitors to encounter the history of the neighbourhood beyond a single monument.

CHAPTER 08

A memory carried into the present

The Blockade Wall remains a place for commemorations and public discussion. Its significance lies not only in the physical site, but in the generations of residents who have worked to preserve and reinterpret the memory of the events of August 1944.
